title: Iain Mapa rides through the night to Muileann dhearg
summary: Word of the fall reaches Muileann chiar by a rider sent without urgency, and Iain Mapa, two seasons into the silver works and no longer reckoned a mine matter by the Board, rides the thirty miles through the night rather than wait for morning, and goes down on the second rope with a lamp and a level.

title: Iain Mapa lays his own old maps against the new fault
summary: With maps sent up from Comann an Airgid's own store, older and truer than anything the Board keeps at Cathair mhòr, Iain Mapa finds the broken ground under the fallen gallery runs exactly where Scàineadh Cill ghlas's own line ran three ages before, marked by an older hand with a single word: left, let be.

title: The thirty-one are buried in a single ground
summary: The dead of the fall are buried at the edge of Muileann dhearg's own burying-yard, thirty-one graves broken in two days by every man in the town not needed underground, the district's custodian reading over each grave in turn at the families' own asking, and Iain Mapa standing the whole of it with his hat in his hand.

title: Sixty apprentices are bound at Achadh dhomhain, and not one is Tuathaich
summary: Comann nan Gualadairean binds sixty boys in its own hall at Achadh dhomhain to fill the rolls the fall thinned by thirty-one, each swearing with a hand laid on a lump of coal while his father stands behind him in a line the length of the hall, and the charter that reserves the oath to Dia-thìreach applicants is kept to the letter.

title: A family with no dead in the fall leaves Achadh dhomhain regardless
summary: Among the forty households that quit Achadh dhomhain for the southern ports that autumn are families who buried no one in the fall, saying to whoever asks that a town may grieve its thirty-one and go on living beside their graves, but a household does not choose to raise its own sons under ground a survey has already misjudged once.

title: Iain Mapa writes a letter naming the fault, and does not send it
summary: At his own table at Muileann chiar, Iain Mapa writes to the Board naming the fault at Cill ghlas by its true line and setting it beside the survey the Board filed and never circulated three years before; he reads it through twice, folds it, and puts it unsealed in the drawer that holds his old receipt.

title: Mary Coyle writes to the Board naming Àth leathan's undelivered timber
summary: Reading a copy of the Board's new digging rules brought north by a carter, Mary Coyle writes in Tional nan Tuathach's own hand asking that the rules be kept in fact at the western pits as well as in the posting, and names Àth leathan and the ordered timber that never left the yard at Ceann mhòr.

title: The Board answers Tional nan Tuathach in three lines and files the matter
summary: The Board thanks Tional nan Tuathach for its concern and states that Àth leathan's timber has been referred to the district overseer for his report; no report is ever filed, and Mary Coyle's letter is kept, unanswered further, in the press at Cathair mhòr where papers go that the Board has no further use for.

title: Ailean Leabhar is found dead at his own desk
summary: On the third day of an t-Sultain, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds Ailean Leabhar at his desk at Muileann chaol, the harvest returns for Siorrachd Doire chaol open under his hand and his pen laid down beside them rather than dropped, so that he seems, she says after, to have finished the line he was writing before he stopped.

title: Ailean Leabhar is buried in the ground behind an Leabharlann
summary: Ailean Leabhar is buried two days after at Muileann chaol, in a small ground behind an Leabharlann itself where no keeper had been buried before him, the town turning out near to the last household, and Mòrag nic Coinnich reads over him only his own words, that an Leabharlann settles nothing and only keeps.

title: Mòrag nic Coinnich finds an unfinished note among Ailean Leabhar's papers
summary: Going through the old keeper's desk in her first month as keeper, Mòrag nic Coinnich finds one sheet in his own hand, undated beyond an old year, reading only that what an Leabharlann is not sent it cannot keep, and to ask the shires again; she cannot say whether it was a note to himself or the start of a letter, and keeps it unfiled in her own drawer.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain is burned beating back the fire with her own cloak
summary: Caught in the fairground when the fire runs on Samhain eve, Oighrig nic Mhathain beats at the burning canvas with her own cloak until the worst of it is turned from the stalls that hold a dozen towns' whole trade, and does not leave the ground until the last flame along the weavers' row has burned itself out.

title: Mary Coyle asks the Board whether its reading of the factor rule is new
summary: When Comhairle na Slighe-iarainn refuses to carry the north's wool on the strength of the fair's own rule on factors, Mary Coyle writes a second, shorter letter asking only whether the reading is new or has simply never before been turned against the north's own goods; the Board does not answer it, and a clerk files it beside the first.

title: The new digging rules sent first to Iain Mapa
summary: The Board's new rules for digging after the fall are sent first to Iain Mapa at Muileann dhearg as the man who closed the district, and he finds nothing in them he would change; they are made for Dia-thìrich workers.

title: Forty households entered 'gone south'
summary: The tally-clerk of Achadh dhomhain enters the forty households leaving for the southern ports off the town's roll with two words against each, gone south, the roll keeping no other word for it.

title: Oighrig nic Mhathain dies of her burns
summary: Oighrig nic Mhathain presides over Cùirt na Fèille from a chair carried into the burnt field, her hands bound in linen, keeps the fair open to its appointed end, and dies of her burns at her own house at Muileann òg before the month is out, fifty years old.

title: The new toll-mistress sells the north's wool through the factors
summary: The new toll-mistress at Muileann òg, keeping the fair's rules as Oighrig left them, sells the north's cart-borne wool through the factors when it comes, and enters the sale in the fair's book under the makers' shire.
